explanations.text:
# DECOMPILE

user asks for a file to decompile

ai harness reads the file and picks an abstraction shape from the kind of file.
it uses [the human skill](compiler/cli/human/skills/human/SKILL.md) and [the shape abstraction catalog](compiler/cli/human/shapes/README.md)]:
  [the rail](compiler/cli/human/shapes/rail.md) if one run.
  [the sections](compiler/cli/human/shapes/sections.md), if a set of functions.
  [the desk](compiler/cli/human/shapes/desk.md), if dispatcher.
  [the dialogue](compiler/cli/human/shapes/dialogue.md), if a rulebook.
ai harness writes the abstraction for [a reader who does not read code](compiler/cli/human/skills/human/SKILL.md:Explain), with pins on the words that name an entity. every other word is free.
ai harness shows the abstraction text and always stop. even if the user message sounded like approval.

user [says the word: map it.](compiler/cli/human/cmd_map.py:e1:cmd_map)

ai harness pipes the exact text into the [human map command using the CLI](compiler/cli/human/cmd_map.py:e1:cmd_map).
the cli verifies the new abstraction and it makes no claude call:
  [it checks the pins point at real code or files](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:build_anchors),
  checks no two pins share their words, [so there are no circular dependencies](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:check_cycle),
  check each block pin gets [its exact lines](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:block_spans).
  a refusal returns the error to the ai harness, which reads it, fixes the text, and runs again.
  words the user wrote himself go in with --verbatim: kept as they are.
    [a pin in them goes in like any pin](compiler/cli/human/cmd_map.py:e1:verbatim_record) when its target exists, and the other pins come after, with the [retext command](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:cmd_retext);
  a copy of them the verbatim, with the pins taken out, stays in the json. called the ["origin"](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:origin_of), so a later mending can be measured against it.
cli creates one new abstaction appended to human/explanation_<path>.json, never updates
  
ai harness [reports](compiler/cli/human/skills/human/SKILL.md:Report): 
  the entry, its pins, the coverage,
  the warnings as if [human show](compiler/cli/human/decompiler.py:e1:cmd_show) was run
  and offer the next abstraction to map:
    a zoom on one block, a file abstraction over the whole, or [the project itself](compiler/cli/human/cmd_project.py:e1:cmd_map_project)

stale.old_text:
import 
  the code reader of python, 
  the line matcher, json, the shell,
  [cmd_map.py](compiler/cli/human/cmd_map.py), [cmd_project.py](compiler/cli/human/cmd_project.py)
  [helper functions](compiler/cli/human/helpers.py),

ANCHOR_RE      = the look of a pin: the words in square brackets, the target in parentheses
SYNC_PROMPT    = the letter to claude when the code changed: read the whole file, mend the words the change made wrong, and add a sentence for each behaviour the change added
STALE_PROMPT   = the letter to claude when the abstractions an entry stands on changed: mend the child's wrong words and carry the new facts down
PAGE_IMPORT_RE = the look of an import in a web page: a from with a path, or a script with a src


finding the pieces of a file

[block_spans](block_spans)(path, lines)
    path is the file on disk; lines is its text, one line each.
    The tool finds every named piece of the file and the lines it covers, so a
    pin can only point at a real piece. A markdown file gives its headings, a web
    page its once-only tags and its functions, a python file its functions and
    classes — read by python's own reader of code. Any other file has no pieces.

[md_spans](md_spans)(path, lines)
    Every heading is a piece that runs to the next heading of the same or a
    higher level. Headings inside a code fence do not count. Two headings with
    the same words stop the run, because a name must point at one place.

[html_spans](html_spans)(path, lines)
    The pieces of a web page, from two hands: [the once-only tags](tag_spans) — a
    tag that opens once, from its opening line to its closing line — and the named
    functions inside every script ([the script regions](script_regions) says where
    the scripts are). A function with the name of a tag stops the run.

[js_spans](js_spans)(path, lines, regions)
    regions are the line ranges of the scripts.
    The tool walks each script, notes where a function starts, and counts the
    braces line by line ([the brace count](brace_delta), which skips braces inside
    quotes and after //) to know where it ends. A function named twice stops the run.


checking the pins of a text

[build_anchors](build_anchors)(text, data, spans, self_id, folder)
    text is one abstraction; data is the map of the file; spans are its pieces;
    self_id is the entry the text belongs to; folder is the project root.
    The tool takes the pins one by one. The words must be there and appear once
    in the text. A pin into the code goes to [the resolving](resolve_code_target);
    a pin into an earlier abstraction must name an entry that exists, an anchor it
    holds, and never its own entry. It gives back the list of checked pins, each
    with its lines. One bad pin stops with the reason.

[parse_target](parse_target)(raw)
    raw is what stands in the parentheses of a pin.
    `e3:the start` is a pin into entry 3's anchor; anything else names a piece
    or a file.

[resolve_code_target](resolve_code_target)(words, raw, spans, folder)
    a piece of this file wins first. 
    then `file:piece` which is a piece of another file of the project. 
    then a file of the project on its own. 
    then a human file on its own, by its bare name
    anything else stops.

[check_cycle](check_cycle)(data, self_id, anchors)
    The tool follows the pins into earlier abstractions, and theirs, and stops
    when the chain comes back to the entry itself. A telling may not stand on
    itself.

[project_pins](project_pins)(anchors)
    if map has no code under it. it doesn't allow a block on itself.
    refuse if pins names another file, block of a file, an abstraction of a file's map or an abstraction in another map with no code under it.


the commands

[cmd_retext](cmd_retext)(a)
    a is what you typed: the file, the entry id, the text or --text, and
    --verbatim. You type `human retext file 2 --text words.txt`.

    ●  the tool checks the new text like a new entry
    │     Every pin real, no two pins with the same words, no circle — and
    │     one thing more: every anchor another entry, or the project map,
    │     points at must still be there.
    │
    ●  the tool looks at whose words they are            ([the gate on your words](verbatim_gate))
    │     With --verbatim the text is yours: the map keeps a copy of it,
    │     with the pins cut out ([the words without the pins](strip_pins)),
    │     as the origin. Without it, an entry that already holds your words
    │     takes new pins but no new word — one changed character, and the
    │     tool stops and tells you to say --verbatim.
    │
    ●  the text goes in place
          When a word changed, each entry that points into this one is
          marked stale, here and in the project map, and the tool names
          them with the line that mends them
          ([the word about the project](report_project_stale)). A text
          that only gained or lost pins marks nobody, and the tool says so.
          An entry that was stale itself stays stale — only the repair takes
          a mark off — and the tool gives the line that mends it.
          Last, the open training session: the row that studies this entry
          [takes a second photo](compiler/cli/human/cmd_train.py:refresh_row)
          of it, so the feed shows the words the map holds now and keeps
          the old ones as v1.

[cmd_undo](cmd_undo)(a)
    The tool removes the last entry of the map, or the entry whose id you
    name ([the entry that goes](undo_target)); an id no entry carries stops
    the run. Three things hold an entry back ([the gate](undo_gate)): an
    entry that others point into stays until they go first; an entry the
    project map points into stays until you retext the project entry — the
    project's own map skips this one; and an entry the open training session
    still holds a row on stays until you close the session. The session is
    the open one of this project — the project id in human/human.json names
    it — and comes from [the training store](compiler/cli/human/cmd_store.py),
    over the network: a machine with no key lets the undo through without this
    last look, and a store that refuses or does not answer stops the run, as
    does a project with no id.

[cmd_show](cmd_show)(a)
    You type `human show file`, or `human show .` for the whole project.

    ●  the tool lists every entry
    │     Id, piece, lines, pins — and the marks: the stale mark names every
    │     explanation the entry waits on ([the stale line](stale_tail)); an
    │     entry of your own words says so, and when the words were changed
    │     since you mapped them it says that too, with the line that brings
    │     them back among the warnings ([the word about your words](verbatim_hint)).
    │
    ●  the tool warns
    │     For every pin that no longer fits its lines, names a piece or a
    │     file that is gone, or points at an anchor that is gone. For a
    │     python file it reads [the imported names](import_names) — plain
    │     imports and the `from .` ones of the same folder — and warns when
    │     a mapped neighbour has no pin in the whole-file entry. For the
    │     project it adds [the doubled lines](dup_warnings): a line of thirty
    │     letters or more that stands in the maps of two files, compared with
    │     pins and punctuation stripped ([the bare line](norm_dup)).
    │
    ●  the tool counts
          How much of the file is covered, and which lines are not.

[cmd_lines](cmd_lines)(a)
    The file with a number in front of every line.

[cmd_sync](cmd_sync)(a)
    You type `human sync file`, or `--old copy.py` when the last version does
    not live in git, or `--stale 3` to mend one dependent entry, or `--for 2`
    to name the entry the code change was written for
    ([the entry the code was written for](written_for)); `--for` with
    `--stale`, or with an id no entry carries, stops the run.

    ●  the tool sees what the change touched
    │     For the project map it only re-resolves the file pins and reports
    │     the gone ones. For a file that did not change it re-resolves the
    │     cross-file pins and stops. Otherwise it holds [the old lines](old_lines_of)
    │     next to the new ones and sees where each line went ([the line map](line_map)).
    │
    ●  the tool names the candidates
    │     Every entry whose lines ([the lines of an entry](entry_lines_set))
    │     the change touched, plus every entry whose piece is gone. An entry
    │     the tool may not reword ([the reword test](rewordable)) — the
    │     whole-file entry with no pin into the code — leaves the list,
    │     unless its piece is gone. The entry named with --for leaves the
    │     list too, unless its piece is gone: the code was written for its
    │     words, so its spans and pins follow and no word changes, and the
    │     tool says so ([the entry that leaves](drop_written)).
    │
    ●  the tool carries every entry and pin to its new lines    ([the re-resolving](re_resolve))
    │     With [the refresh of a file pin](refresh_file_anchor) for pins into
    │     other files. With no candidate it saves and stops — no claude call.
    │
    ●  the tool writes the letter
    │     The diff, the path of the file to read whole,
    │     [the line about the neighbours](touched_note) the file imports, the
    │     pieces, the candidate texts — each named as your own words when
    │     they are ([the mark on your words](verbatim_mark)) —, and the anchors
    │     they must keep.
    │
    ●  claude answers, the tool checks                    ([the rebuild](rebuild_all))
    │     Up to --tries times. Each answer is tried on a copy of the map:
    │     renamed pieces, new texts, every pin checked, every anchor another
    │     entry or the project map needs kept. One broken rule goes back to
    │     claude with its name.
    │
    ●  the map is saved
          The entries that point into a changed one — in this map and in the
          project map — are marked stale, when the words changed and not the
          pins alone. A text of your own words that the sync reworded gets a
          warning that names it ([the word when your words moved](warn_reworded)).
          A candidate that got new lines but kept all its words gets a warning
          that names [the pieces the new lines fall in](blocks_of).

[repair_stale](repair_stale)(a, code_path, root, map_path, data, lines, spans)
    ●  the tool gathers the parents
    │     One stale entry, and for every explanation it waits on the old text,
    │     the new text and the diff between the two ([the page of one
    │     parent](parent_note)); a parent that is gone stops the run.
    │
    ●  the tool writes the second letter
    │     The pages, the dependent's text, and the anchors it must keep — the
    │     pins of the project map among them. An entry that holds your own
    │     words adds one rule: the smallest edit, in your voice
    │     ([the rule about your words](verbatim_rule)).
    │
    ●  claude answers, the tool checks
    │     Up to --tries times; each answer passes the pin checks.
    │
    ●  the map is saved
          Every stale mark goes, and the entry's own dependents, here and in
          the project map, are marked stale when a word changed. A repair that
          changed your words is named on the spot.

[ask_claude](ask_claude)(prompt, root)
    one call to claude with the compiler request; 
    the answer is read as one JSON object.
    tthe compiler request goes in through the pipe, not on the command line, so a long one is never cut short. 
    the call runs in the project root
    a failed call stops the run and shows the reason claude gave.


──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

[stale_notes](stale_notes)(e)                 the stale marks of an entry, always a list

                                              adds a stale mark to the dependents, with the old parent

                                              the entry waits on

                                              keeps a copy of your words, or stops a change of them

                                              says when a sync or a repair changed your own words

                                              one changed explanation for the letter: the old text, the
                                              new text and the diff between the two

[guard_structure](guard_structure)(data, map_path)
                                              stops on a map of the old kind, and makes a lone stale
                                              mark a list

[register_file](register_file)(root, rel)     adds a file to the list in human/human.json
[load_existing](load_existing)(code_path)     the map of a file, or a stop when there is none
[read_text_arg](read_text_arg)(a)             the text from --text or from the pipe; a stop when empty

[print_coverage](print_coverage)(missing, blank, lines)
                                              "covered: 61 of 63 code lines" and the lines left
[report_text_diff](report_text_diff)(eid, old, new)
                                              the changed lines of an entry, - old and + new
[report_project_stale](report_project_stale)(ids)
                                              the line that names the entries of the project map now
                                              stale, and how to mend each

                                              you named
[undo_gate](undo_gate)(root, data, name, entry)
                                              stops an undo that would leave a dependent, a pin of the
                                              project map, or an open training row without its entry;
                                              asks the store for the open session of this project, and
                                              lets a machine with no key through
[written_for](written_for)(a, data, where)    the entry named with --for, checked; a stop with --stale
                                              or with an id the map does not hold

                                              takes the entry named with --for out of the candidates,
                                              unless its piece is gone
